title: Sendai Bank gifts babies their weight at birth in money upon opening a new bank account
description: Having a big baby may be decidedly not fun for the mother, the baby’s first bank account will positively rejoice! content:
Having a big baby may be decidedly not fun for the mother, the baby’s first bank account will positively rejoice!

Beginning on October 1, babies in Miyagi Prefecture can receive celebratory money for being born–and the bigger the baby, the more the money.

Sendai Bank will deposit the equivalent number of yen as the child’s weight in grams at birth upon creation of the first bank account in their name if certain requirements are met. For instance, a baby born at 3,250 grams (7.17 pounds) will receive a gift of 3,250 yen (US$20.59) in their account. The idea was actually devised by an employee, and the bank hopes that this new perk will encourage families to use their services for a long time as the child grows older.

▼ The monetary gift can also be used to help offset the costs of new babies accidentally damaging their parents’ devices.

The main eligibility requirements are that the child is six years or under and received a Sukusuku (“healthy growing”) Box, which is a project being implemented as child-rearing assistance throughout Miyagi Prefecture. The box is filled with helpful childcare items and samples from sponsoring companies. In addition, parents must also deposit a minimum of 30,000 yen into the new bank account at the time of its creation.

For anyone wondering, no, you can’t simply fudge the numbers to make it appear that your baby was born extra chubby. Sendai Bank will confirm the baby’s weight at the time of birth via the official Maternal and Child Health Handbook, a helpful log and guidebook distributed by municipalities that tracks a baby’s growth during pregnancy and post-partum by healthcare professionals. Still, though, if you’re expecting a little one soon, it wouldn’t hurt to try eating some big food before birth to wish for a big bank account.

title: Osaka man arrested for running little pet shop of horrors with dangerous crocodile
description: Your one-stop shop for abused deadly animals. It seems like pet store regulations in Japan tend to be on the lax side. The other day, while taking my daughter through a major home center’s pet section, among the puppies and parrots, I saw a meerkat for sale. What the heck is someone going to do […]
content:
Your one-stop shop for abused deadly animals.

It seems like pet store regulations in Japan tend to be on the lax side. The other day, while taking my daughter through a major home center’s pet section, among the puppies and parrots, I saw a meerkat for sale. What the heck is someone going to do with a meerkat? Are they going to buy some Meerkat Chow at the supermarket?

So, to be a pet store with an illegal collection of animals in Japan, it seems like you have to really put in the effort to lower the bar. That’s just what one resident of Higashiyodogawa Ward in Osaka City had been doing before police finally put a stop to it.

Soma Satomi, the proprietor of a pet shop in the area, was arrested for violating the Act on Welfare and Management of Animals as well as other regulations, after animals such as 21 snapping turtles and a 1.5-meter (5-foot) saltwater crocodile were discovered by police in the store’s back area. In the main area, other exotic animals like bats and scorpions were sold.

The snapping turtles are designated as Specified Invasive Alien Species for the ecological threat they pose in Japan, while the crocodile is a Specified Animal, meaning it poses a potential risk to human life. The crocodile was not yet fully grown, but this species, which has been known to attack humans, is capable of growing to over four meters (13 feet) in length.

▼ A news report about the arrest

The 34-year-old’s pet shop itself hardly seemed up to code either. In fact, when reporters spoke with local residents, very few of them even knew the building sold pets. In addition, the crocodile inside was being kept in an acrylic tank that Satomi appeared to have built himself, measuring only slightly larger than the croc itself at, 150 centimeters long by 61 centimeters high (59 by 24 inches). It was secured by putting a wire mesh over the top of the tank and placing something heavy on top of that.

▼ The location of the pet store. It appears to have been a skateboard shop when this Google Street View images was taken a year ago, but it gives a good sense of how populated the area is.

According to Satomi, the crocodile was his personal pet, and not for sale. That didn’t win him affection from anyone, according to online comments about the news, many of which shuddered to think what could have happened if the animals had escaped.

“I love reptiles, but that is not the behavior of someone who loves reptiles.”
“What was he going to do when he couldn’t take care of them? Abandon them somewhere?”
“Just outlaw pet shops!”
“About 30 years ago, I heard that someone was keeping a cheetah or a leopard at a house near my home. I thought it was a joke, but when I went to see, there really was one pacing around in a wire cage.”
“I once saw this crocodile named Hook at Ueno Zoo during feeding time and was shocked at how high those things can jump.”
“Japan makes it too easy to import wild animals, and the situation allows amateurs to buy and keep them with virtually no oversight.”
“Imagine the flooding Japan’s been experiencing this year happens there. That crocodile would have the run of the town.”

It’s probably safe to say the not-so-unlikely event of a flood occurring and allowing this amphibious apex predator its long-awaited freedom never occurred to its owner. After all, anyone who decided to keep a potentially massive dangerous animal with a lifespan rivaling their own as a pet isn’t especially gifted in foresight.

Hopefully, this particular croc will get a nice, spacious enclosure at a zoo somewhere, where it has all the room it needs to… Well, I guess they do just sit there most of the time, but at least it will have the option of moving around, and that’s what counts.

title: Krispy Kreme Japan gets extra-local with adorable new Hokkaido snow fairy donuts
description: Northern Japan’s heart-meltingly cute birds inspire new mouthwatering sweets. A lot of foreign sweets brands that set up shops in Japan create special desserts that cater to local Japanese tastes, and things get even more focused for Krispy Kreme with its Premium Hokkaido series. content:
Northern Japan’s heart-meltingly cute birds inspire new mouthwatering sweets.

A lot of foreign sweets brands that set up shops in Japan create special desserts that cater to local Japanese tastes, and things get even more focused for Krispy Kreme with its Premium Hokkaido series. These donuts draw inspiration from Japan’s northernmost prefecture featuring not only ingredients sourced from Hokkaido, but which also act as sweet little salutes to the region’s culture and scenery.

So as of October 7, while you can get your sweets fix with one of Krispy Kreme’s original glazed donuts, you can also satisfy your cravings with the adorable new Premium Hokkaido Milky White Shimaenaga.

“What’s Shimaenaga?” and “What’s that thing in the middle of the donut?” are two questions you might be asking, and their answers overlap. The shimaenaga/shima enaga is a species of small bird (roughly 12 centimeters [4.7 inches] in length) that lives in Hokkaido. In winter, their white feathers puff up to help insulate them from the cold, making them look like fluffy little snowballs, and their overall adorableness has earned them the nickname of “snow fairies.”

▼ Shima enaga

The shima enaga, commonly known in English as the long-tailed tit, is a beloved symbol of Hokkaido, and so peeking out from the center of the Premium Hokkaido Milky White Shimaenaga is a snow fairy rendered in milky cream sourced from Hokkaido dairies, with a pair of amanatto (candied red beans) for wings and dots of chocolate for its eyes and beak. The donut itself, meanwhile, has a milky white chocolate coating sprinkled with crunchy bits of white chocolate and silver dragées, evoking thoughts of a glittering Hokkaido winter snowscape.

The Milky White Shimaenaga marks the third time for the snow fairy to be Krispy Kreme Japan’s muse, but this specific combination of flavors is being offered for the first time. As is the norm for the Premium Hokkaido line, it’s exclusive to select Krispy Kreme locations in Hokkaido, specifically the Sitatte Sapporo, Sapporo Pole Town, Sapporo Le Trois, Chitose Outlet Mall Rera, and Mitsui Outlet Park Sapporo Kitahiroshima branches. It’s scheduled to be available from October 7 through late April, and while Hokkaido is a little outside our usual snack run radius, delicious donuts sound like a perfectly good reason to take a trip into Japan’s north.

title: Make-your-own-Totoro plushie workshop event coming to Ghibli Park park this fall
description: Why build a bear when you could build a Totoro? I don’t think it’s really going out on a limb to speculate that “people who want to visit Japan’s Studio Ghibli anime theme park” and “people who want to hug Totoro” are two groups with a whole lot of overlap. I’m not saying the Venn […]
content:
Why build a bear when you could build a Totoro?

I don’t think it’s really going out on a limb to speculate that “people who want to visit Japan’s Studio Ghibli anime theme park” and “people who want to hug Totoro” are two groups with a whole lot of overlap. I’m not saying the Venn diagram of those two demographics is a single, perfect circle, but it’s got to be pretty close, right?

While we’re at it, we can probably say that a lot of people in those largely identical groups would also like to make their own Totoro plushie, and it just so happens that that’s something visitors to the Ghibli Park park in Aichi Prefecture will be able to do next month.

And no, “Ghibli Park park” isn’t a typo. Instead of being a single self-contained facility, Ghibli Park is made up of a number of detached sections which are all within Expo 2005 Aichi Commemorative Park, in the town of Nagakute (near Nagoya). The upcoming Let’s Make a One-of-a-Kind Totoro Plushie workshop is being promoted by Ghibli Park, but is actually being held at the Chikyu Shimin Koryu Center community center, which is also located in Aichi Commemorative Park, just a little north of Ghibli Park’s Hill of Youth area and to the west of the Valley of Witches.

▼ Chikyu Shimin Koryu Center

In the 70-minute workshop, which is open to participants ages 6 and up, you’ll attach your Totoro plushie’s eyes, give him an accessory leaf, stuff him with cotton, sew up the seam along his back, and then be able to take him home to hug at your leisure (or, more likely, begin immediately hugging right there in the park).

Because the workshop isn’t being held within Ghibli Park itself, Ghibli Park tickets aren’t required. However, demand is sure to be high for the total of eight sessions held across two days (10 a.m. and 12:40, 2:20, and 4 p.m. on November 21 and 22), so reservations are being done via an online lottery system administered by Boo-Woo Ticket, the same ticketing service that handles tickets for Ghibli Park. Applications will be open from October 7 to 12, with winners to be notified on the evening of October 16. Up to two reservations can be made per applicant, with a per-person participation/materials fee of 7,000 yen (US$44).

Because the workshops are capped at 32 people, it’s going to take some luck to snag a spot. However, if you aren’t able to take part in the Aichi Commemorative Park sessions, you can take heart in knowing that they’re actually a special traveling itinerary of a regularly held make-your-own-Totoro-plushie event at the Izy Teddy Bear Museum in Shizuoka Prefecture and Nasu Teddy Bear Museum in Tochigi Prefecture.

▼ According to their website, the Izu teddy Bear Museum even lets you make Catbus plushies!

However, making your on Totoro plushie just after or before visiting Ghibli Park does sound like it’d make the experience extra special, and you can find the Aichi event’s reservation application page here.

title: Viral Yokohama cafe tops teas with mini teapots with a clever smoldering secret [Photos]
description: We head to Chazhong for a treat for our taste buds and our eyes. Japan loves all manner of tasty things, but stuff that tastes good and looks good earns a special place in people’s hearts. That presents a special challenge, though, for drink makers, since while a cafe can make its taiyaki fish-shaped cakes […]
content:
We head to Chazhong for a treat for our taste buds and our eyes.

Japan loves all manner of tasty things, but stuff that tastes good and looks good earns a special place in people’s hearts. That presents a special challenge, though, for drink makers, since while a cafe can make its taiyaki fish-shaped cakes surf on waves of ice cream or bake cream puffs that look like Totoro, there’s not much you can do to creatively shape or position liquid refreshment.

But one cafe in Yokohama has been serving up smiles with its beverages, since the cups that its teas come in are topped with little teapots of their own.

The cafe, which opened in Yokohama’s Chinatown this past summer and quickly started generating buzz online, is called Chazhong. Since it’s only about a half-hour from downtown Tokyo to Yokohama, we hopped on the train and rode until Motomachi Chukaigai Station, then took the five-minute stroll over to Koi Koi Yokocho, the food hall that Chazhong is located inside of.

Chazhong has a menu made of up of milk teas using various kinds of Chinese teas, including oolong, white, and pu’er teas, as their base.

That already gives the place a pretty unique concept, but what really makes the place special is that when you purchase your drink ticket from the cafe’s machine, you not only select the size, amount of sugar, and whether you want your tea hot or cold, you also pick between a brown or red teapot…

…which sits on top of your cup’s lid.

That’s not any sort of CG or edited-in visual effect, either. There actually is a wisp of smoke or steam that rises out of the pot.

How does Chazhong pull off this cool trick? At first we thought the teapot might be open at the bottom, and steam was just rising up from the tea that’s inside the paper cup, but that’s not the case.

But the tiny teapot isn’t filled with boiling liquid of its own that steam is rising from either, since it’s too small to heat up on a stove.

However, it turns out there is water inside the pot, plus one other key component: dry ice. That combination produces a whisp of rising smoke that lasts for about 2 minutes, long enough to let you snap some very cook pictures, but not so long that you’ll have to worry about brushing it away while you’re actually drinking your tea,

As for the tea itself, our taste-testing reporter Yayoi Saginomiya’s hot, unsweetened Tieguanyin Tea was smooth with a clean finish, and the richness of the milk provided a special cozy touch to the flavor profile. In hindsight, though, she wishes she’d opted for a cold tea with a little sugar added. Not that her hot unsweetened brew was bad, but it had turned out to be an unseasonably warm day when she visited the cafe, and something cool and sweet would have been a weather-appropriate pick-me-up.

This does mean, though, that she now has a reason to go back again and get the red teapot, since the lid toppers are yours to keep and take home with you.

title: Japanese food hack says to soak your grapes in carbonated water, but is the fizz worth the buzz?
description: We try a Shine Muscat experiment that method claim lets Japan’s most delicious grapes shine in a different way. Shine Muscats don’t really need to be any tastier than they already are. The extra-sweet grapes are among Japan’s most highly prized fruits, and with them in season right now, fans are, quite literally, eating well […]
content:
We try a Shine Muscat experiment that method claim lets Japan’s most delicious grapes shine in a different way.

Shine Muscats don’t really need to be any tastier than they already are. The extra-sweet grapes are among Japan’s most highly prized fruits, and with them in season right now, fans are, quite literally, eating well these days.

Of course, if someone were to figure out a way to make Shine Muscat grapes taste even better, we’d be happy to give it a try, even if it sounded kind of crazy. That’s what we recently did when we tried pickling some Shine Muscats in traditional nukadoko (fermented rice bran), and sure enough, it made their sweetness even more intensely concentrated. The results were so good, in fact, that we were planning to pickle all the rest of our Shine Muscats too, but at the last second, we set some aside for another experiment.

See, we’d also heard rumors that you can enhance your Shine Muscats with carbonated water. We’re not talking about a brief dip in a glass of soda water, either. Japanese foodies who pioneered this technique say you’ve got to let the grapes soak for a long time before you bite into them.

We were curious to try this food hack for ourselves, and the required materials/equipment make for a short list. All you need are Shine Muscat grapes, carbonated water, and a jar with a sealable lid.

Put the grapes into the jar…

…pour in enough soda water to cover them…

…then close the lid tight and let the jar sit in your refrigerator for anywhere between 12 hours and two days.

Shine Muscats are premium-priced fruit, so in the interest of not wasting any for half-effort experimentation, we were patient and held out for the full two days of soaking. When we finally took the jar back out of the fridge and opened it up, all of the carbonation had vanished from the water.

▼ Not a bubble to be seen or a fizz to be heard

We removed a grape from the jar, and set it on a place next to a control-group Shine Muscat that we hadn’t done any sort of treatment to. As you can see in the photo below, the two-day carbonated bath hadn’t done anything to change the grape’s outward appearance.

▼ Shine Muscat soaked in carbonated water for two days (left) and regulae Shine Muscat

Slicing each grape open to look at its cross section, we observed no changes to the carbonated Shine Muscat’s inner beauty either.

The rumors hadn’t said that this experiment would do anything to make the grapes look better, though. The soaking process is supposed to make the Shine Muscats more delicious, so does it? Yes and no, which might sound like faint praise, but we actually were totally satisfied.

As far as we could tell, soaking the grapes in soda water doesn’t change their flavor itself. What it does do, though, is transfer the bubbly quality into the outer layer of the Shine Muscat. Bite into one, and you’re rewarded with a burst of carbonated popping. With the Shine Muscat sweetness still fully present, it’s an incredibly refreshing combination of fun fruity fizziness.

With how simple these are to make, it’d be a snap to whip up a batch of carbonated Shine Muscats either to take to a party or to enjoy as luxurious at-home snacks for yourself. Note, though, that you’ll want to make sure to use a jar where the lid can be shut tightly, since if there’s excess slack in the seal the carbonation is going to escape into the air instead of finding a new home in your grapes.

title: One of Japan’s best convenience store egg sandwiches is one you won’t find at the big three chains
description: Even if you can’t go every day, here’s why you should go to Daily Yamazaki today. content:
Even if you can’t go every day, here’s why you should go to Daily Yamazaki today.

Japan’s big three convenience store chains, 7-Eleven, Family Mart, and Lawson, all sell fine baked goods. The bread is on an especially high level, though, at Daily Yamazaki. Of course, that’s to be expected, what with the chain being owned by Japan’s biggest baking company, Yamazaki Baking Co. So whenever we find ourselves inside a Daily Yamazaki branch, we always make sure to check out what’s stocked in the sandwich corner, and on a recent visit we found one of the best convenience store egg sandwiches we’ve ever had.

Really, most Japanese egg sandwiches could more accurately be called egg salad sandwiches, but Daily Yamazaki’s new Egg Sandwich with a Whole Boiled Egg (or Yudetamago Ikko Shiyo Tamago Sando, in Japanese) is true to its name, and immediately grabbed our attention with its mouthwatering appearance.

Three cross sections are on display, bulging out from between the slices of bread. Though it’s just a single-cut sandwich, as opposed to the more common two-slice varieties, the immense amount of fillings promised a hearty, eggy meal.

The boiled egg is sliced into three pieces, roughly a half and two quarter-sized cuts. And yes, there is egg salad here too, generous slathers that go all the way to the edges of the bread, making this a sort of hybrid-style egg sandwich.

▼ We flipped one piece of bread over to see if Daily Yamazaki skimps on the spread, and were happy to see that they do not.

Taking a bite, we were greeted with a deliciously rich, creamy mixture of egg white and egg yolk flavors, plus an invitingly engaging contrast of the melty egg salad and firmer slices of boiled egg.

It was kind of like eating two different types of egg sandwich at once, an exercise in enjoyable eggy efficiency. If you’re after a more focused experience, though, Daily Yamazaki also has an Ajiwai (“Flavorful”) Egg Sandwich, which finds room to add a dash of spicy dressing to its otherwise conventional egg salad filling, again with so much that it’s practically overflowing from the bread.

But even with the Whole Boiled Egg sandwich being a touch more expensive than the Ajiwai (334 yen [US$2.10] versus 284 yen) it’s hard to say no to something that looks and tastes so good, and we highly recommend it for your next cholesterol cheat day.

If you’ve got Totoro in your Ghibli-loving heart, why not have him on your lap too?

Now that we’re past the fall equinox, we’ve got increasingly long nights and chilly weather on the temporal horizon. So Totoro is arriving just in time with a new way to help keep you feeling warm and fuzzy, in both the literal and figurative senses, as we head through fall and into winter.

Studio Ghibli anime specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku has just unveiled their latest blanket design. Dubbed “Sound of the Starry Sky,” the blanket’s pattern features all three Totoros, big, medium, and small, perched in the treetops as the big guy and his midsize brethren have an ocarina jam session.

At 100 centimeters (39.4) inches in length and 70 centimeters in width, this a lap blanket, not sized for use as bedding, but something to curl up cozily with while lounging on the couch. Alternatively, you could take the Totoros to work with you, if your office happens to set the thermostat lower than you like.

▼ The design includes the movie’s title, My Neighbor Totoro, written in Japanese.

Along with the new Sound of the Starry Sky version, Donguri Kyowakoku has also restocked a number of its previous blanket designs featuring Totoro, the Catbus, Soot Sprites, and even Jiji, for fans of Kiki’s Deliver Service.

As with the Totoro ocarina blanket, these are all available as 100 x 70-centimeter lap blankets.

However, some of the patterns are also offered as “half blankets” (140 x 100 centimeters) and the three patterns below even come in 200 x 140-centimeter full-size versions too.

Prices start at 3,300 yen (US$21) for the lap blankets, while the half-blankets are 5,500 yen and the full-sizes either 7,700 or 8,800 yen, depending on exact pattern (order links below). So far there’s no word as to whether the Sound of the Starry Sky will be getting larger versions at some future date, but even if it stays on your lower body, it’s sure to warm your heart all the same.

title: Foreign tourist numbers drop in Osaka, despite record-setting highs from U.S. and Korea
description: Almost every country is sending more travelers to Osaka these days, with one very big exception. With the international travel community still showing an intense interest in visiting Japan, you’d think Osaka’s inbound tourism numbers would be booming. It’s Japan’s third largest city, is situated close enough to Kyoto to be used as a livelier […]
content:
Almost every country is sending more travelers to Osaka these days, with one very big exception.

With the international travel community still showing an intense interest in visiting Japan, you’d think Osaka’s inbound tourism numbers would be booming. It’s Japan’s third largest city, is situated close enough to Kyoto to be used as a livelier place to spend the night after a day of visiting shrines and temples, and it’s also a stop on the popular Sanyo Shinkansen line, making it easy to work Osaka into itineraries along Japan’s “golden route” of top travel destinations for foreign visitors.

And yet, Osaka actually saw fewer foreign visitors this past August than the city did in August of 2025, according to statistics compiled by the Osaka Convention and Tourism Bureau.

At first, the data might not sound like it’s going to lead to that result. In August of 2026, Osaka had more visitors than it ever has in any previous August from the U.S., South Korea, Taiwan, France, Hong Kong, Indonesia, and Russia. In addition, more tourists from Italy and Spain came to Osaka in August of 2026 than in any other month before.

But even with all those individual-demographic records being set, Osaka still had a 9.6 percent drop in foreign visitors during August 2026 compared to August 2025. So what country has been shunning the city?

China. August tourist numbers from mainland China plummeted 59 percent compared to last year. 254,000 Chinese travelers still showed up, but the drop was so severe that it more than cancelled out the total 26.7-percent August increase in travelers from all foreign countries other than China.

The cooling off in demand from Chinese travelers stems from a warning issued late last year by the Chinese government cautioning its citizens that Japan is an unsafe country to travel to. It should be noted that this warning wasn’t prompted by any actual incident of Chinese travelers being injured or robbed in Japan, but it did come right on the heels of Japan’s prime minister Sanae Takaichi saying in an interview that Japan would provide aid to Taiwan if it were to be invaded by the Chinese military.

With international travel generally requiring advance reservations, there wasn’t an immediate drop-off in travelers from China, but new reservations started coming in with less frequency, and when we ourselves went to check in on how things were in Osaka last December (when we took the photos seen in this article), we definitely noticed much smaller crowds in parts of the city that had, up until then, been routinely packed with Chinese tourists.

“It is a very dire situation,” said Osaka Convention and Tourism Bureau chairman Hitoshi Mizohata at his regularly scheduled press conference on September 30.

▼ And yes, he delivered that somber proclamation while wearing a plushie of Osaka Expo mascot Myaku-Myaku.

Without access to Osaka travel and tourism providers’ books, it’s hard to say exactly how truly dire the situation is. Obviously, a roughly 10-percent drop in customers isn’t something that any industry is going to be happy about. At the same time, that’s not a catastrophic dip, especially considering that tourist numbers have grown far more than 10 percent compared to where they were before the international Japan travel craze. So unless the travel industry went all-in on building excessive capacity because they thought the boom times were never going to so much as slow down, they should still be doing much better financially than they used to, even if their profits aren’t quite as high as they were last August.

That said, Mizohata voiced his concern that the Chinese government hasn’t made any statement reversing its “safety” warning about traveling in Japan, and so the board has no estimation of when, or if, Chinese tourist numbers will rebound. Mizohata lamented that political disagreements aren’t being kept separate from economics, though this is hardly the first time in history for those two social sciences to affect each other.

Overall, it’s probably still too early to shed all that many tears for the travel industry in Osaka. Mizohata says that local hotels have told the bureau that they have more reservations for October and November in 2026 than for the same period last year, and premium-priced hotels reportedly are especially receiving lots of bookings. The bureau also says that, based on surveys with foreign tourists in Osaka, there’s still room to better promote awareness of Osaka’s nightlife, traditional culture, sports, and luxury leisure offerings, and it plans to increase its focus on those areas

title: Starbucks Japan says sayonara to the Filone for new sandwiches and a Pumpkin Soupuccino
description: Things are changing at Starbucks, but is it for the better? While the spotlight at Starbucks tends to shine firmly on the drinks in Japan, there are a lot of delicious meals on the menu too. One food option that had a lot of love from locals was the Filone sandwich, with filone being a […]
content:
Things are changing at Starbucks, but is it for the better?

While the spotlight at Starbucks tends to shine firmly on the drinks in Japan, there are a lot of delicious meals on the menu too. One food option that had a lot of love from locals was the Filone sandwich, with filone being a longish Italian sourdough bread with a crispy crust and airy crumb. This rustic bread reflected the Italian-influenced baked goods served up at the chain’s in-house Princi Bakery, but now the chain has surprised everyone by ditching the Filone and replacing it with a baguette instead.

The Filone has long been one of Starbucks’ signature food items, holding centre stage in the sandwich display case for around 18 years, so we stopped by to find out if the switch was a good decision.

▼ Having loved the Filone for many years, we picked up the new product with equal measures of curiosity and apprehension.

We chose to try the Ham & Gouda Cheese Baguette Sandwich (540 yen [US$3.42]), which seemed closest in taste to the Ham & Maribo Cheese Filone we used to pick up on a regular basis, and we also picked up the “Herb Sausage”, which we also used to enjoy as a Filone.

▼ We also couldn’t resist trying the Pumpkin Soupuccino (500 yen) as well, which was released on the same day.

Starting the taste test with the Soupuccino, so named as it’s a frothy, cappuccino-like soup, we took a sip and found it had a creamy pumpkin taste. Made with onion and celery, and pumpkins sourced from Hokkaido, a famous producing region, the soup was finished with spices like black pepper and nutmeg before being frothed up to give the bold flavours a light and airy mouthfeel.

▼ Maple flavour, added as a secret ingredient, gave each sip a soft sweetness, creating a cosy cup of soup that was as delicious as it was comforting.

With our palate warmed up, literally and figuratively, it was now time to try the baguette sandwiches, starting with the Ham & Gouda Cheese. At first glance, it looked to be a little smaller than the Filone, and at around 15 centimetres (5.9 inches) in length, it looked like a long baguette cut in half.

Still, it had the same elongated look as the Filone sandwiches, so the appearance didn’t strike us as too different, but after taking a bite, the difference became clear. The big change was in the texture of the bread, which was moist and chewy, with a beautifully toasted surface. It was slightly softer than usual, and it also seemed to contain more filling, with a generous amount of ham paired with the mild, melty Gouda cheese.

▼ This is a worthy replacement for the Filone.

Another welcome change is that this product is now eligible for the Good Start! Morning breakfast discount. The Filone version wasn’t eligible, so this is a welcome new development for anyone who likes to start their mornings with a coffee and a sandwich.

▼ The Good Start! Morning deal gets you a 40-yen discount when you buy an eligible food and drink item together before 11 a.m.

▼ Finally, we took a bite of the “Herb Sausage”.

Surprisingly, the flavour of the filling seemed no different to the Filone version, which we were very pleased about, as the taste of herbs was on point, making every bite a delicious one.

▼ Again, the baguette did a great job, pairing exceptionally well with the juicy, meaty filling.

Though we started the taste test with a slight sense of sadness at the Filone’s disappearance, by the end of it all, we had fallen head over heels for the baguette sandwiches. According to Starbucks, the baguettes are made with a new, high hydration dough to make them softer than before, and the change really is noticeable. The soft bread pairs wonderfully well with the soft fillings, melding together to create some seriously moreish sandwiches.

After trying two of the savoury versions, we’re now keen to try the Chocolate & Butter version, which sounds like the perfect partner for the new Pikachu Honey Cream Latte.

title: Totoro and other Ghibli anime figure humidifiers return just in time for the dry season [Photos]
description: Three ways to deal with uncomfortably dry weather while also letting you go “Ahhhh! Isn’t Totoro/Calcifer/Jiji cute?” Japan has a love/hate relationship with humidity. content:
Three ways to deal with uncomfortably dry weather while also letting you go “Ahhhh! Isn’t Totoro/Calcifer/Jiji cute?”

Japan has a love/hate relationship with humidity. Once the rainy season starts in mid-June, you can be certain to hear people murmuring, or even groaning “Mushimushi shiteiru ne?” (“It’s so humid, isn’t it?”) until about the mid-point of September. Then, pretty much as soon as the autumn weather gets cool enough to be considered crisp, many people will start to say how the air is uncomfortably dry.

Having grown up in the atmospherically arid environment of Southern California, I’m honestly totally fine with the level of dryness in Japan during the fall and winter. As such, I’ve never personally seen much appeal in a humidifier, but even I can understand that if someone did want one, they’d want one of these awesomely adorable Studio Ghibli humidifiers.

These seasonal products are back in stock once again at Ghibli specialty shop Donguri Kyowakoku. The full lineup consists of three designs, and naturally we’re starting with a look at the Totoro one.

The water reservoir topper features both a big and small Totoro, with the larger forest spirit playing his ocarina, which the steam billows out of as the water is heated.

▼ There’s a trio of shy soot sprites too!

Each of the humidifiers stands 27 centimeters (10.6 inches) tall, with a base roughly the size of a drink bottle or thermos. That compact footprint makes the Little Humidifiers, as Donguri Kyowakoku calls them, suitable for use even in compact work/study spaces or other cozy nooks of your home.

Going form forest spirits to a fire one, joining Totoro in humidifier form is Calcifer, from Howl’s Moving Castle.

Calcifer’s design lends itself even more naturally to use as a humidifier, with the steam rising out from underneath the frying pan of on his back making it look like he’s right in the middle of cooking up that bacon-and-egg breakfast.

And rounding out the group is Jiji, the black cat companion of the titular heroine of Kiki’s Delivery Service.

Jiji’s topper also has a clever place that the steam rises from, as it comes out of the coffee mug he buys while shopping with Kiki as they set up her new apartment, creating the illusion that someone has just poured a fresh cup of java.

▼ Warning! Although Donguri Kyowakoku makes no official mention of the phenomenon, be aware that using the Jiji humidifier will almost certainly make you crave pancakes.

The humidifiers are identically priced at 5,280 yen (US$33) and come bundled with their USB power cord. They’re designed to automatically shut off after eight hours of continuous use, but since the bottles are also sized to hold enough water to humidify for eight hours too, once that much time passes you’ll need to refill the bottle anyway.

The entire lineup can be purchased through the Donguri Kyowakoku online store here, and if you could use even more Calcifer in your home, these days he’s a cool candle nightlight too.

title: Casio collaborates with a Kyoto foil master for a luxurious one million yen G-SHOCK
description: Featuring inspirations from kigumi wood joinery design and hand-dusted platinum, each of these limited edition watches are a unique work of art. Bringing a fusion of ancient Japanese artistry and modern engineering to the wrists of elite collectors and timepiece connoisseurs, Casio will introduce a new member on November 13 to its flagship MR-G line […]
content:
Featuring inspirations from kigumi wood joinery design and hand-dusted platinum, each of these limited edition watches are a unique work of art.

Bringing a fusion of ancient Japanese artistry and modern engineering to the wrists of elite collectors and timepiece connoisseurs, Casio will introduce a new member on November 13 to its flagship MR-G line in celebration of three decades since its inception in 1996. Priced at 1.1 million yen (around US$7,350), and limited to only 800 pieces worldwide, MRG-B2100HR-1A has its design centered around the theme of haruka, a Japanese concept conveying timeless strength and boundless duration.

At the heart of the watch’s artistry is kigumi, a traditional Japanese woodworking and architectural technique where timber is joined without nails, other metal fasteners, or adhesives. The woodworkers intricately carve joints that connect seamlessly and have no possibility of corrosion. Reinterpreting this into watchmaking, the dial forms an intricate, three dimensional lattice.

Above this marvel of construction, renowned metal leaf artist Hiroto Rakusho applied his craft by hand. Born in Kyoto’s Nishijin district, Rakusho is an officially designated Traditional Craftsman known for expanding Nishijin foil art onto global stages and contributing to digital archiving for cultural preservation.

Rakusho personally decorated each 3-D dial using sunago, a technique originating in the creation of picture scrolls and Buddhist texts, where platinum leaf is ground into a powder before being dusted over a surface. The delicate, uneven distribution of platinum creates a brilliance and deep gradation that exhibits itself uniquely on every single piece, guaranteeing that each watch has its own artistic fingerprint.

To mirror Rakusho’s artwork on the exterior, Casio applied structural color technology via ultra-short pulse lasers across the bezel and watchstrap. The micron-level laser texturing mimics the natural iridescence seen on butterfly wings and mineral crystals, producing a colorful beauty that changes depending on the viewing angle.

Complementing this is Casio’s advanced metal construction: an octagonal bezel, based on the popular MRG-B2100, crafted from 27 individually polished components, alongside premium COBARION (a cobalt-chromium-molybdenum alloy about two times as hard as stainless steel, and which has a platinum shine) and DAT55G (a high-performance titanium alloy, around three times that of pure titanium) alloys that provide structural resilience.

By capturing the spirit of haruka, the MRG-B2100HR-1A unites Kyoto craftsmanship with modern engineering into an enduring piece of wearable art.

title: Opening of new Gundam anime superstore in America postponed indefinitely
description: Gundam Base Minneapolis grand opening has been derailed by “unforeseen circumstances.” September 30 was supposed to be a day of joy, excitement, and plastic for fans of venerable anime mecha franchise Gundam. That’s because it was the date on which the grand opening of Gundam Base Minneapolis, a brand-new Gundam superstore, was scheduled to take […]
content:
Gundam Base Minneapolis grand opening has been derailed by “unforeseen circumstances.”

September 30 was supposed to be a day of joy, excitement, and plastic for fans of venerable anime mecha franchise Gundam. That’s because it was the date on which the grand opening of Gundam Base Minneapolis, a brand-new Gundam superstore, was scheduled to take place inside the Mall of America in the northern U.S.

Unfortunately, the day turned out to be one of, if not necessarily sadness or full-on disappointment, a decided lack of new Gunpla models to put together, because not only did Gundam Base Minneapolis end up not opening on September 30, as of right now no one knows when the store will be open.

▼ Artist’s preview rendering of Gundam Base Minneapolis

As announced through Bandai Namco’s American website and official Twitter account, the store’s grand opening had to be delayed “due to unforeseen circumstances.” Not only that, it’s been delayed indefinitely, with no word as of this writing as to when it will be ready for shoppers and event guests.

Bandai Namco was able to give fans a heads up four days before the scheduled opening, so that no one had to waste a trip to the location just to find its doors closed. Also effected is the Bandai Namco Cross Store, an anime and character merchandise specialty shop, which will be located adjacent to Gundam Base Minneapolis. The Cross Store was also supposed to open on September 30, an event which has similarly been postponed indefinitely.

To its credit, Bandai Namco has been rather courteous in handling the matter, saying in its announcement:

We deeply apologize for any inconvenience this change may cause.

We know many of you have been looking forward to exploring these new destinations, and we’re just as excited to welcome you through our doors. We’ll share the new opening date as soon as it is confirmed, along with more details about what you can expect when we open.

We sincerely apologize again and thank you for your patience, understanding, and continued support.

Unfortunately, with no more specific details about the cause of the delay than “unforeseen circumstances,” it’s impossible to even speculate how long the delay may be, though it’s hard to escape the feeling that Char is somehow involved.

title: McDonald’s Japan officially changes its mascot’s name…to Ronald McDonald
description: Yep, that’s actually a change for McDonald’s Japan. On October 1, McDonald’s Japan shocked fans with a surprise announcement that they’re changing the name of the chain’s mascot. Some might say it’s crazy to throw away decades of name recognition for such a widely recognized spokescharacter, but McDonald’s Japan feels like the time is right, […]
content:
Yep, that’s actually a change for McDonald’s Japan.

On October 1, McDonald’s Japan shocked fans with a surprise announcement that they’re changing the name of the chain’s mascot. Some might say it’s crazy to throw away decades of name recognition for such a widely recognized spokescharacter, but McDonald’s Japan feels like the time is right, and posted on its official Twitter account that that the famous clown decked out in the company’s red and yellow colors will, from now on, be known as Ronald McDonald.

▼ 今日からロナルド = “From today, I’m Ronald.”

ドナルド、どーなるの？ pic.twitter.com/y97RsfnVTH

— マクドナルド (@McDonaldsJapan) October 1, 2026

To many of our readers, this might seem like old news. Like, 63-year-old news, since 1963 was the year when McDonald’s friendly clown character made his debut in U.S. TV commercials for the fast food chain, and in which people clearly said his name was Ronald McDonald.

However, ever since Japan’s first McDonald’s opened in 1971, he’s been known here as “Donald McDonald.”

It’s not exactly clear why Ronald got a new leading consonant for his name while crossing the Pacific. One theory is that Den Fujita, the Japanese businessman who established McDonald’s Japan, thought that “Ronald” would be difficult for Japanese people to pronounce. However, the Japanese language has both “ro” and “do” sounds, and “ro” isn’t at all a rare sound within Japanese names or vocabulary, so it’s not a particularly difficult sound for native Japanese speakers to make. Another possible explanation that’s been posited online is that the change to Donald was made to avoid confusion with Ranald MacDonald, who in 1848 became the first native English speaker to teach the language in Japan. Despite the important role he played in the country’s history, though, Ranald MacDonald is far from a household name in Japan, and as much as modern-day McDonald’s Japan likes wordplay, it seems doubtful that they’d feel compelled to rename their mascot to cater the sensibilities of linguistics enthusiasts.

▼ An anime-style Donald McDonald, showing off his “Donald magic” powers. Sadly, the animation doesn’t seem to have been produced by Studio Pierrot (yes, I do cater to the sensibilities of linguistics enthusiasts).

But whatever the reason, back in 1971 McDonald’s Japan said hey, we like this clown character you’ve created, but we’re gonna rename him Donald, OK? And perhaps because no one knew the character was going to stick around this long, or because the fast food industry was still young enough that chains weren’t thinking about global branding synergy, Ronald became Donald in Japan, until McDonald’s Japan’s announcement that he’s now Ronald.

The character’s “From today, I’m Ronald” tweet has drawn comments such as:

“Biggest shock of the year.”
“Naw, dude you’ve been Ronald since a long time ago.”
“They’re not renaming him Ronald McRonald, are they?”
“Now people are gonna be able to tell how old you are if you say ‘You know, he used to be called ‘Donald.’”
“It’s going to take me some time to get used to this.”
“I mean, we’re all going to keep on calling him ‘Donald,’ right?”
“I think he didn’t want to have the same first name as Trump.”
“People in Japan know him as Donald, so they should have kept it like it was. There’s no need to go out of the way and match his name in other countries.”

Regarding the last two comments, though McDonald’s Japan did, a very long time ago, print “Donald Trump” cards (“trump” being what Western-style playing cards are called in Japan) featuring their mascot character, when the current U.S. president comes up in conversation in Japan, his first name is rarely used, so it’s unlikely that Donald McDonald’s name was changed to avoid association with Donald Trump.

On the other hand, McDonald’s Japan apparently does think there’s a good reason for matching the name used for the character in other countries, and it’s not necessarily to sell more burgers. On the same day that McDonald’s Japan announced that their mascot’s name is now Ronald, the Donald McDonald House Japan charity organization said that it is renaming itself to Rondald McDonald House Japan, in order to more clearly convey its alignment with the goal of helping children battling illnesses or other medical conditions shared by the many Rondald McDonald House divisions in other countries.

▼ Rondald McDonald House Japan announcing its new name

日本にハウスができて、25年。
私たちは、新たな一歩を踏み出します。

名称やロゴは変わりますが、
病気と向き合う子どもとそのご家族の
「第二のわが家」としての使命は変わりません。

「#家族いっしょ」 の力を信じて― #ロナルドマクドナルドハウス は、
これからも、支える家族を支え続けます。 pic.twitter.com/Wh0PxDOp8M

— 公益財団法人ロナルド・マクドナルド・ハウス・ジャパン (@dmhcj) October 1, 2026

As for McDonald’s Japan’s customers needing some time to get used to Ronald’s new name, we can relate, but we think they’ll come around eventually, especially as long as the chain doesn’t tinker too much with its tsukimi burger recipe.

title: Starbucks Japan keeps the Pumpkin Spice Latte alive this autumn
description: Seasonal exclusive graces the menu for a limited time, proving pumpkin spice isn’t dead in Japan. For Starbucks customers in the U.S., the Pumpkin Spice Latte has been going strong as an autumn special for 23 years, but here in Japan, it’s still a baby, having only become a regular seasonal addition since 2021. content:
Seasonal exclusive graces the menu for a limited time, proving pumpkin spice isn’t dead in Japan.

For Starbucks customers in the U.S., the Pumpkin Spice Latte has been going strong as an autumn special for 23 years, but here in Japan, it’s still a baby, having only become a regular seasonal addition since 2021.

So although customers overseas may be tiring of the flavour, with some claiming pumpkin spice is dead as people turn to other trending drinks like matcha, here in Japan customers still have a strong thirst for it. In fact, it remains so popular that the beverage is making its return for another season, in hot and iced versions, with members of the Starbucks Rewards program getting an early taste of it on 29 September, a day ahead of its official release.

▼ The Pumpkin Spice Latte is available in Short through to Venti sizes, priced from 550-680 yen (US$3.50-4.33).

As always, the drink is inspired by the flavors of pumpkin pie, combining the gentle sweetness of the autumnal vegetable with warming spices, and a dash of nutmeg as a flourishing finish. A good serving of milk adds a smooth richness to the mix, creating a mellow flavour that’s ideal for colder nights and shorter days.

It’s nice to see the Pumpkin Spice Latte returning to the menu, because although matcha is popular here, pumpkin spice has an overseas quality that makes it a unique novelty for Japanese customers. It’ll be particularly special to get a taste of it while kicking back in one of the country’s newest and most interesting stores, but as always, it’ll only be on the menu for a limited time through autumn.

title: Japanese Shinto ceremonial sand-digging in London celebrates start of British Library expansion
description: Swapping out scissors and ribbons for sand and farm tools. Japanese property developer Mitsui Fudosan recently held a groundbreaking ceremony for its historic £1.1 billion (approximately 230 billion yen [US$1.46 billion]) expansion of the British Library in London, and in doing so also brought a long-standing Japanese tradition to the other side of the world. […]
content:
Swapping out scissors and ribbons for sand and farm tools.

Japanese property developer Mitsui Fudosan recently held a groundbreaking ceremony for its historic £1.1 billion (approximately 230 billion yen [US$1.46 billion]) expansion of the British Library in London, and in doing so also brought a long-standing Japanese tradition to the other side of the world. As an institution boasting one of the largest book collections on earth, the British Library is expanding its footprint near its main building across the street from London’s St. Pancras International Station. As part of Japan’s largest scale real estate development to date in the UK, Mitsui Fudosan and the British Library are looking to construct a multi-story complex housing commercial offices, rental laboratories, and expanded library facilities.

To mark the start of work, UK government officials, library leadership, and Mitsui Fudosan executives gathered for a chakko-shiki (“groundbreaking ceremony”), more formally known as a kiko-shiki. Major property developments in Western countries often center around a simple ribbon-cutting, but construction in Japan traditionally has an entire sequence of ceremonies designed to ensure safety, prosperity, and community goodwill.

These Japanese construction customs traditionally start with a jichinsai, a sacred Shinto purifying ritual led by a Shinto priest. This religious ceremony uses offerings of rice wine, salt, and rice to pacify the local tochi-no-kami (earth deities), asking permission to alter the land and praying for protection against construction accidents or natural disasters, as well as for the prosperity of those who will use the land. In modern times, not all chakko-shiki begin with a jichinsai, with some people favoring to simply recognize the secular business side of the ceremonies, but the British Library event included this splash of tradition, featuring a non-Japanese Shinto priest who participated in the ceremony.

There are of course talks by the key people involved in the construction project, but the highlight and prime photo opportunity of the event is the ugachi-zome (literally “first pierce”), the symbolic first dig, where these important people grab a hoe or shovel and stab them into a small mound of sand.

Historically, preparing for building a house in Japan was a three-step process: clear the area of weeds, dig up the soil, and level the ground, and it is said that a house cannot be built without this process. Therefore, the full Shinto groundbreaking ceremony has evolved into three parts, starting with kari-some (“the first cut”), where the designer cuts grass with a sickle.

▼ The “ey, ey, ey” is very much an intergral part of all three parts.

This is followed by the kuwaire-no-gi (“hoe entry ceremony”), where the client lightly chips out a section of sand from the mound with a hoe.

Then comes the sukiire-no-gi (“shovel entry ceremony”), where person in charge of construction flattens the mound with a shovel (suki, 鋤), or at least makes more of a dent than with the hoe.

The other aspects of the jichinsai are also embedded with history and religious meaning and culminate in the naorai, the closing feast in which participants share the sake and food that were offered to the deities in order to receive their blessings, before then returning to daily life (naoru means “to return”).

Other ceremonial rituals continue through the stages of a building’s construction lifecycle, such as the joto-shiki, or raising-the-ridgepole ceremony, when the main structure is complete. Historically, carpenters placed symbolic items on the highest beam meant to ward off disaster and pray for good fortune, but nowadays it has been streamlined to just a sacred wooden wand or wooden plaque containing the names of the master carpenter, the homeowner, and the deities invoked in protecting the house, which is permanently sealed away within the roof cavity.

The four corners of the building site are splashed with ceremonial sake and salt to purify the land, and ensure the safety of both the workers and future residents.

In some instances of residential development, the whole neighborhood gets together for a mochi-throwing event, sometimes substituted with coins or sweets, in a bid to foster goodwill with the neighbors who will live alongside the development.

At the end of larger-scale construction projects, when the entire building is finished, stakeholders assemble for a shunko-shiki (construction completion ceremony), which announces the completion to the public, conveys gratitude to those physically and financially involved in the construction, and prays for safety and prosperity.

With the jichinsai and chakko-shiki being performed at such a large-scale overseas investment project, we’ll have to wait and see if they complete the entire trio of construction ceremonies at the British Library’s expansion, and find out whether or not they’ll climb to the top floor and start lobbing down tea bags in place of mochi, in an attempt to build goodwill with the locals.

title: Kyoto announces two-tier admission price plan for Nijo Castle, non-residents would pay twice as much
description: First-of-its-kind system for Kyoto would raise maintenance funding and fight overtourism, proponents say, but will it really reduce crowd sizes? Many of Japan’s castles were built by a local samurai lord, but Kyoto’s Nijo Castle is an exception in that it was built specifically for use by out-of-towners. Constructed in 1624, Nijo Castle, and the […]
content:
First-of-its-kind system for Kyoto would raise maintenance funding and fight overtourism, proponents say, but will it really reduce crowd sizes?

Many of Japan’s castles were built by a local samurai lord, but Kyoto’s Nijo Castle is an exception in that it was built specifically for use by out-of-towners. Constructed in 1624, Nijo Castle, and the attached Ninomaru Palace, were the Kyoto residence of Tokugawa Ieyasu, founder of the Tokugawa shogunate, and his heirs, a place for them to stay when they rolled into Kyoto on official business from Edo (as Tokyo was called in those days).

However, starting next year out-of-towners are probably going to be paying twice as much to get into the castle, as Kyoto’s mayor Koji Matsui has announced plans for a two-tiered admission system.

Currently, the combined ticket for Nijo Castle and Ninomaru Palace is priced at 1,300 yen (US$8.15). Under the new system, the admission price for residents of Kyoto City would be reduced, down to just 1,000 yen, while non-residents of the city would pay double, 2,000 yen. “By raising the admission price [for non-residents], additional funds can be applied to maintenance,” said Matsui, “and hopefully our city’s residents can more easily come visit the castle.” The new pricing structure would make Nijo Castle the first tourism facility in the city with a two-tier admission system.

It’s no secret that even among Japan’s major tourism attractions, no other city in the country is feeling quite as overtouristed as Kyoto is these days, with a growing sense that the city’s atmosphere and the lifestyles of local residents are being disrupted. To illustrate the amount of visitors Kyoto has been receiving, in 2025 2.07 million people visited Nijo Castle, but only about 2 percent of them were Kyoto City residents.

However, while Kyoto is filled with more international visitors than ever before, Nijo Castle’s two-tier pricing system wouldn’t charge the higher price exclusively to foreign tourists. Domestic Japanese travelers who don’t live in the city would also pay 2,000 yen for admission, even those coming from other cities within Kyoto Prefecture.

All else equal, the reduced ticket price for residents will make it easier, financially speaking, for Kyotoites to visit Nijo Castle. It’s unlikely, though, that charging out-of-towners more is going to significantly improve overcrowding. Again, there are two groups of people who would be paying the 2,000-yen admission, Japanese residents of cities other than Kyoto, and foreign tourists. For foreign tourists, many of whom have been drawn to Japan at least in part by the weak yen, having to pay an extra 700 yen, equivalent to less than US$4.50, probably isn’t going to make anyone cross Nijo Castle off their itinerary. That price increase is going to feel like more of a demotivating factor to Japanese domestic travelers, but for many of them Kyoto has already lost a lot of its allure as a sightseeing destination, what with the prevailing image of Kyoto these days being that it’s packed with foreign tourists and prices for hotels have skyrocketed, so at most it’d be a situation of a dip in numbers from an already deflated demographic.

Matsui says the draft ordinance for Niko Castle’s two-tier ticket system will be formally introduced at a city council meeting next month, and would go into effect in the spring of next year.

title: Japan announces new permanent residency guidelines, foreigners must earn more than average Japanese person
description: Japanese government suddenly raises income bar for foreigners seeking permanent residency, will apply new rules even to applications filed six months ago. On Thursday, the Japanese government announced new guidelines for foreigners seeking permanent residence in Japan. Under Japan’s Immigration Control Act, foreign nationals seeking to become permanent residents of Japan must satisfy three conditions. […]
content:
Japanese government suddenly raises income bar for foreigners seeking permanent residency, will apply new rules even to applications filed six months ago.

On Thursday, the Japanese government announced new guidelines for foreigners seeking permanent residence in Japan.

Under Japan’s Immigration Control Act, foreign nationals seeking to become permanent residents of Japan must satisfy three conditions. They must demonstrate good conduct (i.e. not break any laws) and have financial assets/job skills that will prevent them from becoming a burden on social welfare programs. Finally, the applicant’s permanent residency status must be determined to serve Japan’s national interests.

Those are all broadly defined conditons, and the Japanese government’s new interpretation of them is going to significantly raise the bar for displaying financial security. Until now, an annual income of roughly 3 million yen (US$19,000) was considered to be a baseline, but generally acceptable, amount for a permanent residency applicant. 3 million yen isn’t a lot; it’s more or less a typical salary for a low-level office job in Japan. Still, with proper budgeting and a frugal lifestyle, it’s enough to make ends meet.

Under the new guidelines, however, foreigners will have to show that they earn an annual income above the national average for Japanese citizens. It’s unclear whether this is referring to the applicant’s individual income or that of their household as a whole, but according to government statistics the average unmarked adult income in Japan is approximately 4.5 million yen, bringing minimum required income up by 50 percent. The increase is even larger if evaluators are going to be using the average household income for Japanese citizens, which is 5.8 million yen.

But hey, if those foreigners who want to obtain permanent residency status can’t pull themselves up by their bootstraps and double their income, they can just file their applications before the new guidelines go into effect, right? Nope. The government announced the new guidelines on October 1, and said that the higher-than-average-Japanese-citizen income requirement will be applied to permanent residence applications filed as of April, but that’s not April of next year. No, the new income guideline is being retroactively applied to applications that were submitted as much as six months ago.

▼ It seems unreasonable to make the only alternative to the retroactive increase be to travel back in time and file your application on an earlier date, seeing as how even the wealthy struggle to find usable time machines.

Two other criteria are set to change from this coming April, one of which involves the amount of time a foreigner who’s married to a Japanese citizen has to live in Japan before they can obtain permanent residency. Currently, the couple must have been married for at least three years, and the foreign spouse must have lived in Japan for at least one year in order to be eligible. From April, those requirements are going to be lengthened to the couple having been married for five years, and the foreign spouse having lived in Japan for at least three. Note that these requirements are in addition to the above income requirement, not a substitute for it.

Foreign residents who are not married to a Japanese citizen will need to have lived in Japan for 10 years in order to be eligible for permanent residency, an amount of time which is unchanged from the current system. The 10-year residency requirement is going to be a moot point for many younger applicants, though, because from April evaluators will also be looking at permanent residency applicants’ projected pension benefits, with the new guidelines saying applicants should have benefits equivalent to those of someone who has been paying into Japan’s national pension system for 30 years.

All of this is taking place against a backdrop of Japanese residents dealing with the most severe price inflation in generations for basic goods and services, while also seeing more and more foreign tourists spending carefreely while on vacation in Japan. At the same time, Japan’s foreign resident population has increased, but as the majority of them are working for Japanese employers and getting paid in yen, they’re not reaping the benefits of the weak yen that foreign tourists are. Foreign residents can still make easy scapegoats for frustrated Japanese nationals who feel like their standard of living is eroding, though, and with foreign residents of Japan not being able to vote, it’s not surprising that politicians going to bat for them on this matter are in short supply.

Aside from playing to the preferences of a certain segment of the voter base, it’s hard to see how the new guidelines will actually benefit Japan. The required 30 years of pension benefits is likely to have a negative affect on younger foreigner’ interest in relocating to Japan, since it would involve taking on the risk of potentially spending their prime working years in Japan without knowing whether they’ll be able to settle in the country permanently until they hit their 50s. That, in turn, lessens the potential for immigration to help counteract the negative effects of Japan’s falling birthrate and shrinking total population. Raising permanent residency requirements isn’t going to do anything to help Japan attract the world’s best and brightest expats, either. The stricter guidelines don’t do anything to benefit them, and between Japan’s lower salaries for executive positions compared to overseas companies, plus the weak yen, high-flying professionals can earn significantly more working elsewhere, then enjoy the best of what Japan has to offer to wealthy leisure tourists without really needing to reside in the country.

But hey, at least if foreign residents are unable to obtain permanent residency under the new guidelines, at least they can look forward to paying higher fees when they have to renew their visas.

Source: Mainichi Shimbun, Asahi Shimbun

title: Japanese scientists grow sheet of heart muscle cells for world’s first general-patient ReHeart-ing
description: Patient had a new piece of her own heart attached to her old one. You may even remember back in 2006, when Shinya Yamanaka announced that he had converted […]
content:
Patient had a new piece of her own heart attached to her old one.

We often report on scientific and medical breakthroughs that have the potential to change the world, but more often than not, they seem to just disappear. You may even remember back in 2006, when Shinya Yamanaka announced that he had converted mature skin cells into pluripotent stem cells, cells which are capable of taking on any function. These induced pluripotent stem (iPS) cells even won Yamanaka the Nobel Prize in 2012.

But after that, not much came of it outside of research labs, until 29 September, when the world’s first commercialized iPS treatment, ReHeart, took place at Osaka Police Hospital. ReHeart was developed by Osaka University Professor Emeritus Yoshiki Sawa and his biotech startup Cuorips and involves creating a sheet of heart muscle cells from iPS cells and applying it to the heart of a patient suffering from severe heart disease.

▼ ReHeart muscle sheets and a model of a functioning heart made from 200 million iPS cells were on display at the Osaka Expo last year.

The treatment was approved by the Ministry of Health, Labour and Welfare with the condition that its efficacy is verified in the next seven years. Having been tested on eight people in the past, the first general patient was a woman in her 50s who suffered from severe heart failure after having a heart attack. The surgery took about 50 minutes, and no problems were reported.

Sawa acknowledged that 20 years was a long wait for the practical application of this medical discovery, but even that was only achieved through the hard work of medical professionals as well as the support of private companies and the government. He hopes things will be able to move forward more quickly from this point onward.

Readers of the news, however, expressed a great deal of impatience in online comments, especially when it comes to potential iPS treatments for their own personal afflictions.

“That’s great and all, but how about making some hair! HAIR!!!”
“We’ll need to create tooth, hair, and kidney regeneration next.”
“It’s only gotten this far?”
“When will we see the regeneration of optic nerve bundles and retinas?”
“I would like to have two more arms.”
“I wish they could make something that cures cold sores instantly.”
“I wish they had sheets of brain cells too.”
“Dr. Yamanaka… It’s time… to talk about hair.”
“Baldness isn’t life-threatening, so it’s on the back burner.”

Though iPS cells do have the potential to restore hair growth, the cost would probably be astronomical. Estimates for ReHeart are upwards of 15 million yen (US$96,000), but Japan’s national healthcare systems would only require a patient to pay about 30 percent of that, with further reductions made based on their age and income.

However, ReHeart is simply a sheet of uniform heart muscle cells, whereas recreating even a single hair follicle is considerably more complex, with multiple different types of cells working in unison. Also, since it’s not a life-threatening condition, insurance won’t cover hair-growth therapy, requiring the patient to pay the full amount. Needless to say, anyone seeking new hair this way will have to pay an arm and a leg, and then pay again for a new arm and leg generated by iPS cells.

On the bright side, another treatment that was approved alongside ReHeart was Amchepry, dopaminergic neural progenitor cells created from iPS cells and used to help restore motor function to patients with advanced Parkinson’s disease.

Seeing effective treatments for these two illnesses that inflict pain and suffering on millions of people around the world is encouraging, and better late than never.

Source: YTV News, Itai News, Cell & Gene Therapy Review
